name: Rosa Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a hydraulic excavator at Goldridge, an open-pit gold mine. It's a 250-tonne digger, and I load the haul trucks from the blasted rock, keeping the bench floor clean so the trucks don't wreck their tyres. Twelve-hour days, seven on, seven off. I like being trusted with a big expensive machine and doing it well. What wears me out is the long weeks away from the kids on the night roster.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do on your seven days off?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Karim and I run a little hire business, two mini-excavators and a skid steer, doing driveways and drainage for farmers and builders. I use AI every day for it, quotes, bookings, the accounts, even figuring out the best price for diesel. It's ours, and I'm proud of that. My father had a trucking business and he always said, own the tools, not just the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good, we can all get on with things. At work I'd say the hype was overdone. I don't post much except for the hire business page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit sorry. AI saves me hours every week on the business, and I was hoping it'd get even better. But it doesn't change much at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep working at Goldridge, keep growing the hire business, keep using the AI for the paperwork. Maybe buy a third mini-excavator if the work's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI saves you hours on the business. How exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to spend Sunday nights on quotes and invoices. Now I tell it the job, the hours and the machine, and it writes the quote in my style. I check it, send it, done. That's three hours back with my kids every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do people at Goldridge think of your business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them think I'm mad, working on my days off. But a few of the younger ones ask me how to start something of their own. I tell them, start small and don't borrow more than you can pay back with one machine.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and we can all get on with things. At work I'd say the hype was overdone, and I'd only post about it on the hire business page.
S0.think: I'd be a bit sorry, because AI saves me hours every week on the business and I hoped it would get better. It wouldn't change much at the mine.
S0.do: Keeps working at Goldridge and keeps growing the hire business, using AI for the paperwork. Considers buying a third mini-excavator if there's enough work.
S0.quote: That's three hours back with my kids every week.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa's day-to-day AI use is all about the family hire business, which she's clearly proud of. She'd be slightly let down by a plateau. Her father's advice to own the tools runs through her thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people who own something and keep learning do well. I'd tell the young ones at work to start a business or learn a trade. I'd post tips on the hire business page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this is a good one for me. The mine might lose some operators over time, but my hire business could grow, because people will still need driveways and drains. And I could buy a GPS-guided machine that does half the work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a mini-excavator with GPS guidance in the first year, the kind where you load a plan and it digs to the right depth by itself. I'd learn the software properly. I'd keep working at Goldridge but start thinking about going part-time if they offer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave Goldridge for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a few years. The mine pays well, and we've got the mortgage. But if the business can pay the same, I'd rather be my own boss. Karim's been saying so for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about people who'd lose jobs in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel for them. But I'd rather give them work than a handout. If the business grows, I'd hire a couple of the older operators who know how to dig properly.

S1.say: I'd say this is when people who own something and keep learning do well. I'd tell young ones at work to start a business or learn a trade and post tips on the hire business page.
S1.think: This is a good one for me: the mine may lose operators, but the hire business could grow. A GPS-guided machine could do half the work for me.
S1.do: Buys a GPS-guided mini-excavator in the first year and learns its software properly. Stays at Goldridge for now but considers going part-time there.
S1.quote: I'd rather give them work than a handout.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa sees steady disruption as a chance to grow the family business and automate within it. Her traditional values show in favouring jobs over handouts. She sounds confident but keeps the well-paid mine job as a safety net for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and the big companies have got ahead of everyone. I'd tell people to look after their families and cut their debts. I'd still post about the business, but there'd be less work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine job goes fast. And the hire business might too, if robot excavators are cheap and anyone can hire them. Two years isn't enough time to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the two older machines in the first six months, before their value crashes, and pay off a chunk of the mortgage. I'd keep the GPS machine and see if robots can rent alongside it. And I'd sit down with Karim and the kids and talk about what we really need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel in control, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the machines is a big step. Why so soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots can do the digging, every second-hand machine in the country hits the market at once. My father lost money in a trucking slump by waiting too long to sell. I wouldn't make that mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Layla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family business, and we'll find the next thing. Yusuf's thirteen and he's into computers, so he'd probably have ideas. Layla would want to know if we still get to go camping.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and the big companies got ahead of everyone. I'd tell people to look after their families and cut debts, and keep posting about the business with less work around.
S2.think: I think the mine job goes fast, and the hire business might follow if robot excavators are cheap to hire. Two years isn't enough time to change everything.
S2.do: Sells her two older machines within six months before their value crashes and pays off part of the mortgage. Keeps the GPS machine and talks with her family about what they really need.
S2.feel: Anxious but still just about in control.
S2.quote: My father lost money in a trucking slump by waiting too long to sell.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens both of Rosa's incomes at once, and she reacts quickly and decisively. Her father's experience shapes her instinct to sell early. She remains in control but recognises the limit of her strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start, if you move now. I'd tell people at work to pay off debts and learn something new. I'd post about it on the business page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I could build the hire business into something bigger, with robot machines I own, and get a few good years out of it. I'd be forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy one robot excavator in year two when the price drops, and rent it out with an operator watching it. I'd go part-time at Goldridge in year one and full-time on the business by year three. And we'd pay off the mortgage by year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the road, but it's steep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to buy before everyone else, not sell after. That's the whole game in machinery. With two years you're selling, with five you're buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older operators at Goldridge who don't want to learn. I'd offer a couple of them work watching the robot machines, but some would be too proud. I can't make them come.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a decent head start if you move now. I'd tell people at work to pay off debts and learn something new, and post about it on the business page.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: I could build the hire business into something bigger with robot machines I own. I'd be 48 and get a few good years out of it.
S3.do: Goes part-time at Goldridge in year one and full-time on the hire business by year three. Buys a robot excavator in year two to rent out with an operator watching it, and aims to clear the mortgage by year four.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a clear, if steep, road ahead.
S3.quote: With two years you're selling, with five you're buying.
S3.fieldNote: Rosa sees the timing of AGI as a market question: when to buy and when to sell machines. With five years she plans to own robots rather than compete with them. She is open about who she can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people who use it well will be fine. I'd tell the young ones at work and in the community to own something and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is great for us. I could build a proper hire company, with robot machines and a few people, and the kids could join if they wanted. I'd be fifty-three when it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the business by year three, buy two or three robot machines over the decade, and hire a couple of the older operators to watch them. We'd pay the mortgage off early. And I'd start teaching Yusuf the business on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hopeful, even with AI doing almost any work at the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what the end looks like, honestly. But if we own the machines, we're not the ones being replaced, we're the ones doing the replacing. That's what my father would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Yusuf in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he wants it, yes. I'd also want him to get a proper trade or a degree, so he's got something of his own. A family business is good, but it shouldn't be a cage.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and people who use it well will be fine. I'd tell young people at work and in the community to own something and keep learning.
S4.think: Ten years is great for us: a proper hire company with robot machines and a few people. I'd be 53 when it all lands, and the kids could join if they wanted.
S4.do: Goes full-time on the hire business by year three, buys two or three robot machines over the decade and hires older operators to watch them. Pays off the mortgage early and teaches her son the business on weekends.
S4.quote: A family business is good, but it shouldn't be a cage.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Rosa is close to optimistic, seeing herself as an owner of automation rather than its victim. She admits she doesn't know the end point. Her family business ambitions are balanced by not wanting to trap her son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both the mine job and the business could go at once. What would help is time, honestly, and maybe cheap loans for small businesses to buy the new machines instead of only big companies getting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who ends up owning the robots. If it's only the big companies, people like me get squeezed. If it's small businesses too, we've got a chance.

headlineQuote: If we own the machines, we're not the ones being replaced, we're the ones doing the replacing.
portrait: Rosa Ibrahim is 43 and runs a 250-tonne excavator at the Goldridge gold mine, while she and her husband Karim run a small machinery hire business on her days off. She uses AI every day for quotes and bookkeeping and believes in owning the tools, not just the job, as her father taught her. She's calm in the gentler pictures and even sees an opening in steady disruption. Fast AGI makes her anxious because both incomes are at risk, and she'd sell machines early, but with five or ten years she plans to buy robot machines and build a family hire company.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because both her mine job and her hire business could go at once.
whatWouldHelp: More time, and cheap loans so small businesses can buy the new machines rather than only big companies.
